content.title: Communications outage: family reconnect
content.summary: Calls aren't getting through and your household is spread across town. Walk through how you'd find each other.
content.objective: Practice reconnecting with your household when phone calls aren't getting through.

sources.label: American Red Cross — Make a Plan
Ready.gov — Hurricanes (staying in touch after a disaster)

communicated_clearly.text: You reached out with a short, clear message instead of waiting on calls.

used_out_of_area_contact.text: You gave everyone one out-of-area contact to check in with.

used_household_plan.text: You leaned on what your household had already agreed on.

recognized_official_source.text: You checked official sources before acting on a rumor.

needs_contact_review.text: Make sure your household has an out-of-area contact, written down as well as saved in phones.

needs_meeting_place_review.text: Agree on a meeting place everyone knows, before you need it.

nodes.title: Calls aren't connecting
nodes.body: A major storm moved through this morning. Your household is safe but spread across town, and phone calls keep failing.
nodes.prompt: How do you reach your household first?

choices.label: Send a short text: "I'm safe. Where are you?"
choices.feedback: Texts may get through when calls don't, and they can save battery. Ready.gov suggests saving phone calls for emergencies after a disaster.

choices.label: Keep calling until a call connects
choices.feedback: Phone systems are often down or busy after a disaster. Ready.gov suggests text messages or social media to reach family, and saving calls for emergencies.

choices.label: Post "We're okay" where your family will see it
choices.feedback: Ready.gov lists social media, along with texts, as a way to reach family and friends when phone systems are busy.

nodes.title: Only some replies come back
nodes.body: A text arrives from school: "here, phone at 20%". Your other messages show as not delivered.
nodes.prompt: How do you keep track of who's okay?

choices.label: Ask everyone to check in with your out-of-area contact
choices.feedback: The Red Cross notes it may be easier to text or call long distance when local lines are overloaded. One shared contact gives everyone the same place to check in.

choices.label: We don't have an out-of-area contact yet
choices.feedback: That's worth setting up on a calm day. The Red Cross recommends choosing one, because long-distance texts and calls may get through when local lines are overloaded.

choices.label: Keep resending to each person
choices.feedback: Resending can work. A shared check-in contact means everyone reaches one person instead of everyone trying everyone.

nodes.title: Finding the numbers
nodes.body: Without one person everyone checks in with, you'll need to reach people one by one.
nodes.prompt: Where do you look for the numbers you need?

choices.label: The contact card we keep in our wallets and bags
choices.feedback: Written contacts still work when a phone is out of battery or lost. The Red Cross recommends everyone carry emergency contacts in writing.

choices.label: Search my phone and try to remember the rest
choices.feedback: Phones run out of battery. The Red Cross recommends carrying emergency contacts in writing as well as saving them on your phone.

nodes.title: Where do we meet up?
nodes.body: Another adult in your household finally replies: "Phone almost out of battery. Where do we meet up?"

choices.label: "Our meeting place from the plan."
choices.feedback: A meeting place everyone already knows means nobody has to work it out under stress. Ready.gov recommends one that's familiar and easy to find.

choices.label: "Let's decide when we can talk."
choices.feedback: Deciding later is harder when phones are spotty. Ready.gov recommends setting a familiar meeting place ahead of time.

choices.label: "Call me and we'll work it out."
choices.feedback: Their battery is low. Ready.gov notes texts may be more reliable than calls and can save battery power.

nodes.title: A post about the phones
nodes.body: A neighbor shares a post saying phone service will be out for three days. It doesn't say who it's from.
nodes.prompt: How do you find out what's actually happening?

choices.label: Check official alerts and what local officials are saying
choices.feedback: Ready.gov advises paying attention to local officials for information and instructions. Wireless Emergency Alerts aren't affected by network congestion.

choices.label: Forward the post to your household
choices.feedback: A post with no source may not be right. Ready.gov points to local officials and official alerts for information and instructions.

outcomes.title: Your household reconnected
outcomes.body: You used what you had and kept everyone in the loop. That's what practice is for.

outcomes.title: Your household reconnected
outcomes.body: Everyone found each other. Next time, check official sources before passing news along.
